results.title: The Brontë Sisters: Anne Brontë and The Tenant of Wildfell Hall
results.content: # The Brontë Sisters: Anne Brontë and The Tenant of Wildfell Hall *“…how cruelly he has trampled on my love, betrayed my trust, scorned my prayers and tears, and efforts for his preservation, crushed my hopes, destroyed my youth’s best feelings, and doomed me to a life of hopeless misery, as far as man can do it, it is not enough to say that I no longer love my husband – I* HATE *him!”* I am a huge Brontë fan. While Charlotte, Emily, and Anne often get lumped together, they had fairly distinct voices. Author of *The Tenant of Wildfell Hall,* Anne Brontë was the youngest Brontë sister. It was Charlotte’s idea to publish their poetry, and after funding their own book, they then moved on to writing novels. Anne died at 29, only months after her siblings Branwell and Emily succumbed to tuberculosis. In a way, that’s surprising, given that her second novel, *The Tenant of Wildfell Hall,* was shocking when it first came out. The story begins as an epistolary, where a farmer named Gilbert writes letters to his best friend about Helen, a mysterious young widow who has moved into the nearby Wildfell Hall with her son, Arthur. When their son is born, Huntingdon gets jealous of all the attention Helen gives him, and he begins an affair with a woman he was courting at the same time he’d courted Helen. Helen finds out about the affair, tells Huntingdon she wants to leave him, but he won’t have it. That is apparently the reason why Anne’s big sister wanted to keep *The Tenant of Wildfell Hall* quiet. Also, while all three Brontë’s wrote under male pen names, at one point the rumors were that Charlotte, or the author of *Jane Eyre,* also wrote *The Tenant of Wildfell Hall*, and that infuriated her. Sadly, when Anne died not long after her novel’s release, Charlotte limited any further editions. Truthfully, I find *Jane Eyre* and *Wuthering Heights* more entertaining than *The Tenant of Wildfell Hall,* mostly because Helen is so pious, it’s not as easy to connect with her as with passionate Jane or Catherine.

ANNE BRONTË (1820–1849), pseudonym Acton Bell, was an English poet and novelist, the youngest daughter of the Reverend Patrick and Maria Brontë and younger sister of Charlotte and Emily. Because of family finances, Anne worked as a governess for several years and was a keen observer of the life of those with wealth and privilege, noting what she saw as the lack of morality they espoused. Anne never married and died at the age of 29 from tuberculosis.Anne wrote two novels: *Agnes Grey* (1847) and *The Tenant of Wildfell Hall* (1848). Anne’s mission in her writing, as she said in the preface to the second edition of *The Tenant of Wildfell Hall*, was “to tell the truth, for truth always conveys its own moral to those who are able to receive it … I would rather whisper a few wholesome truths therein than much soft nonsense.” ## Additional information ## Reviews There are no reviews yet. results.content: ## The Tenant of Wildfell Hall Summary. # The Tenant of Wildfell Hall Summary. In the first part of the epistolary novel, told by letters of the protagonist Gilbert Markham to his friend Jack Halford, Markham describes the arrival to Wildfell Hall of a mysterious woman dressed in mourning a long time ago. At the cries of her son soon runs scared Mrs. Graham; she coldly thanks Gilbert and does not hide her distrust of him. But the little Arthur, son of Mrs. Graham, who on the contrary, imbued with confidence in Gilbert, forces them to come to terms. Jane’s hatred is not groundless as well - the owner of Wildfell Hall, Mr. Lawrence, who she has feeling for, pays Mrs. Graham too much attention. However, Helen (the name of Mrs. Graham, as Gilbert discovers only after long acquaintance with her) firmly rejects all his advances. However, Gilbert returns to Wildfell Hall, and, to his misfortune, sees Helen walking in the garden with Mr. Lawrence. Soon Gilbert notices that his conduct brings Helen suffering and goes to Wildfell Hall. When Helen learns about the infidelity she demands Arthur to let her go with her son to live separately, but Arthur refuses, not wanting to spoil his reputation. The situation seems hopeless, but then Helen’s brother Frederick comes to the aid, he is ready to give his sister shelter in Wildfell Hall, an empty mansion in which they were born and lived as children. One early autumn morning Helen, with her son and faithful servant, Rachel flees from her husband's house and safely gets to Wildfell Hall. #### The Tenant of Wildfell Hall Questions and Answers.
